body:
Systolic array (matmul accelerator)

The matmul accelerator is a 16×16 systolic array. It tiles each matmul internally onto the 16×16 array, and it also enables tiling at the software level, so matrices larger than the array are split into tiles in software and run as a sequence of matmuls.

Measured throughput on the DE1-SoC (N×N int8 matmul), systolic array vs CPU baseline:
- 64×64: 6.043 vs 1.255 GOP/s (4.82×)
- 128×128: 11.392 vs 1.382 GOP/s (8.24×)
- 256×256: 18.302 vs 1.442 GOP/s (12.69×)
- 512×512: 18.884 vs 1.454 GOP/s (12.99×)

Full table: ECE496 Files & Data → Matmul throughput: CPU baseline vs systolic array.

MNN backend / TinyViT integration (Nov 3, 2026)

The full TinyViT model runs on the DE1-SoC with one attention matrix multiplication offloaded to the FPGA; the remaining operations run on the CPU. Both synthetic test inputs and six physical matrix tests passed.

In single-run tests, offload made full-model inference 5.74% faster on zero input and 2.71% slower on nonuniform input. A reliable speedup and accuracy on real images are not yet established.

Next: repeat matched benchmarks, measure offload overhead, and test accuracy on real images.

WIKI Update

- Added editable member updates, biweekly team summaries, and meeting notes.
- Organized project results, Gantt chart, and ECE496 files into dedicated tabs.
- Added in-page forms to create, edit, and remove entries.

SIMD Measurement

- Tested 32×32 int8 matrix multiplication on the board’s Cortex-A9 CPU.
- Compiled with GCC, using -O3 -mcpu=cortex-a9 -mfpu=neon.
- Compared plain C code with NEON SIMD, using the same calculations and quantization.
- Used 1,000 warmup runs and 10,000 timed runs, then compared median times.
- Plain C took 202.12 µs; SIMD took 94.67 µs, making SIMD 2.13× faster.
- SIMD results matched the plain C reference.

Softmax Implementation

- Built 16-bit fixed-point softmax, supporting up to 196 values per row.
- Used a lookup table to calculate exponential values, with 3,073 useful entries stored in 4,096 × 16 bits (8 KiB).
- Changed division to use restoring unsigned division, which calculates one bit per clock cycle and finishes in 33 clock cycles, reducing hardware usage and improving timing.
- Tested 147 rows and 8,666 outputs; all results exactly matched the Python integer reference.
- The standalone module passed 90 MHz timing and used 222 ALMs and 10 M10K memory blocks.
- Next step: connect softmax to the matmul accelerator and test the complete system.

GELU Integration and Timing

- Confirmed bias + GELU is connected to accel_top and processes results when the CPU reads the output buffer.
- Supports 16 int8 values at once, with a 256-byte bias buffer that the CPU can load.
- The standalone module now passes 90 MHz timing; logic usage dropped from 1,707 to 957 ALMs.
